overview.text: The Alamo, in downtown San Antonio, began in 1718 as Mission San Antonio de Valero, one of several Spanish Franciscan missions along the San Antonio River. After moving to its present site in 1724, it grew into a community with a chapel, priests’ residence, homes, workshops, and irrigation ditches. Secularized in 1793, it later served as a military post. During the Texas Revolution, Mexican troops besieged the fortified compound for 13 days and captured it on March 6, 1836; the defenders’ deaths made the Alamo a powerful rallying symbol, but the battle did not end the war. The origin of its name is disputed: it may honor the soldiers’ former company or refer to nearby cottonwoods.

key_facts.text: The mission’s work involved Indigenous communities; Spanish authorities also used missions to advance territorial claims in Texas.
Two proposed explanations for “Alamo” are the name of the soldiers’ former company and the Spanish word for cottonwood; the name’s origin is uncertain.
The 1836 garrison included Tejanos as well as Americans, Anglo-Texians, and other European immigrants; families and enslaved people were also inside.
The chapel and Long Barrack are among the best-known surviving structures; much of the original mission compound is now beneath city streets and buildings.
The battle became a symbol of sacrifice and a rallying cry in the Texas Revolution; the war continued after the Alamo fell.
